638.title: Vibhishana's crossing
638.hook: the enemy's brother asks to be let in; the camp argues; Rama makes a vow
638.howItsDone: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition the Vibhishana episode is taught as the model of śaraṇāgati, taking refuge, and Rama's vow in Yuddha Kanda 18 is recited and commented on as a central verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vibhishana told Ravana the truth, was called a disgrace, and crossed the sea. Your line: I've come for refuge.

A war camp on a beach, the eve of battle. A figure appears in the sky above it, with four armed companions, and calls down: I'm the enemy king's brother, please let me in. Sugriva, king of the monkeys, doesn't hesitate. He goes straight to Rama: this is a trick. He's a rakshasa, Ravana's own brother, and he'll strike when we're not looking. Kill him, or send him away. The whole camp starts arguing.
screen: `A FIGURE IN THE SKY.` → `THIS IS A TRICK.` → `THE CAMP ARGUES.`

segments.voice: Rama asks his council, and Valmiki lets every voice speak. Angada says test him first. Others say send a spy, or question him closely. Jambavan is suspicious of the timing. Then Hanuman speaks, the one who has actually been inside Lanka. He came openly, not in disguise. I've watched his face, and I see no deceit in it. He knows Ravana's wrongs and has seen your strength. Accept him. Then Rama gives his answer. I can't turn away someone who comes as a friend, even if he has faults. And then something larger. Anyone who comes to me even once and says, I am yours, I give safety from every being. That is my vow. Sugriva still pushes back. Rama goes further. Even if it were Ravana himself, bring him in. In the Sri Vaishnava tradition of South India, this verse is treasured as a teaching on sharanagati, taking refuge, or surrender: the one who turns to God even once, sincerely, is held. Others read it more plainly, as the code of a good king toward someone asking for protection. Then Rama does something practical and startling. He has Vibhishana come down, sends for sea water, and pours it over his head, consecrating him king of Lanka, right there on the beach, before a single battle has been fought.

Let the door in your chest open by one inch; breathe in and notice the caution, breathe out and notice the welcome, and let both be there.

639.title: the siege
639.hook: two spies dressed as monkeys are caught in Rama's camp, and he lets them go
639.howItsDone: Storytellers often use the release of Shuka and Sarana to show the code of war in the Ramayana: an unarmed messenger or captive is not killed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vibhishana's crossing. Rama vowed safety to anyone who comes even once and says I am yours, and crowned Vibhishana on the beach. Even if it were Ravana.

The army crosses the bridge and spreads out along Lanka's shore. Across the island, Ravana does what any general would. He sends two of his ministers, Shuka and Sarana, to count the enemy. They take the shape of monkeys and slip in among the troops. It almost works. But one person in that camp knows exactly what a rakshasa in disguise looks like, because he grew up among them. Vibhishana sees through them, and they're dragged before Rama.
screen: `THE ARMY IS ACROSS.` → `TWO SPIES DRESSED AS MONKEYS.` → `VIBHISHANA SEES THROUGH THEM.`

segments.voice: In a war story, you know what usually happens to caught spies, and the monkeys are ready to do it. The two rakshasas, terrified, confess: Ravana sent us to count your army. And Rama laughs. If you've seen everything, he says, go back. If there's anything you missed, look again; Vibhishana will show you around. You're unarmed and you were caught. You won't be killed. Then he gives them a message. Tell Ravana: show me the strength you relied on when you carried Sita away. Tomorrow he'll see my arrows fall on his city. The spies go home and tell Ravana the truth, the last thing he wants to hear. Valmiki then gives a long scene on a high tower. Ravana looks out over the enemy camp, and Sarana points out the leaders one by one: Nila, Angada, Nala, Hanuman, Jambavan, Sugriva, Rama and Lakshmana. Their advice, after all that, is to make peace and return Sita. Ravana is furious and throws them out. A siege is a contest of fear. Ravana wanted information, and Rama gave him more than he asked for, so he'd know exactly what was coming. Mercy and confidence arrive together. And the spies who came to count soldiers go home telling their king to make peace.

640.title: the siege
640.hook: a king who leaps into a fight, a messenger who won't be held, and the gates of Lanka
640.carry: peace offered, even at the gates
640.howItsDone: In North Indian Ramlila performances, Angada's embassy to Ravana's court is a well-known scene, often played in the Ramcharitmanas version with Angada's unmovable foot.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the siege began with two spies caught and set free. Rama hid nothing, and they went home urging peace. Nothing to hide.

Rama climbs Mount Suvela with his leaders to look at Lanka. And there, on a high tower across the way, stands Ravana himself, in royal clothes, among his attendants. Sugriva can't stand it. Without a word to anyone he leaps across, lands on the tower, knocks off Ravana's crown, and the two kings wrestle. Then Sugriva jumps back, pleased with himself. Rama is not pleased. A king doesn't do that, he says. If something had happened to you, what would I have done?
screen: `RAVANA ON HIS TOWER.` → `SUGRIVA LEAPS ACROSS.` → `A KING DOESN'T DO THAT.`

segments.voice: Then Rama does things in order. Lanka has four great gates, and he assigns a leader to each: Nila to the east, Angada to the south, Hanuman to the west, and Rama himself, with Lakshmana, to the north, where Ravana is. The city is surrounded. And still, before the first blow, Rama sends a messenger: Angada, Vali's son. Angada leaps to Ravana's palace and speaks plainly: return Sita, ask pardon, and you'll live. If not, this is the end of your line, and Vibhishana will rule Lanka. Ravana orders him seized. Four rakshasas grab him by the arms. Angada lets them. Then he springs onto the palace roof with all four still hanging on, and they drop off and fall to the ground. He stamps on the roof's peak, breaks it, and leaps back to Rama. You may know a different scene here: Angada planting his foot in Ravana's court, and no one able to lift it. That comes from later tellings, especially Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. In Valmiki it's the broken rooftop. Either way, Rama made a final offer of peace, in person, with the city already surrounded. Only after Angada returns does the battle begin. The monkeys swarm the walls with trees and rocks, the rakshasas pour out of the gates, and the siege of Lanka becomes a war.

641.title: Indrajit's arrows
641.hook: a warrior nobody can see, arrows from an empty sky, and the brothers fall
641.howItsDone: Ramayana tellers often slow down at the serpent-arrows, the nāgapāśa, letting listeners sit with the heroes' fall before the rescue comes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the siege. Lanka's four gates surrounded, Angada carrying one last offer, and then the battle began. Peace offered, even at the gates.

The first day of fighting goes badly for Lanka. Duel after duel, the monkey and bear leaders win, and the rakshasa champions fall or run. The sun sets, and the fighting goes on in the dark, by the light of weapons. In one duel, Angada smashes the chariot of Ravana's son, killing his horses and driver. The prince jumps clear. Then he does something the monkeys have no answer for. He disappears.
screen: `A GOOD FIRST DAY.` → `FIGHTING IN THE DARK.` → `HE DISAPPEARS.`

segments.voice: His name is Indrajit: conqueror of Indra, king of the gods, and the epic says he earned it by once carrying Indra off as a captive. His birth name was Meghanada, the one who roars like a thundercloud. Now he rises out of sight among the clouds and starts shooting. The arrows come out of an empty sky, and nobody can tell where to aim back. These aren't ordinary arrows. Valmiki says they turn into serpents as they strike, wrapping Rama and Lakshmana tight. Snake after snake, arrow after arrow, until the two brothers can't move. They fall side by side, covered in shafts like a bed of arrows. Sugriva, Angada, Hanuman and Jambavan gather around, stunned, staring at the two men they came to fight for, lying still. Indrajit, invisible, shouts down that he's killed them, and goes home to tell his father. What makes this frightening isn't only the power. It's that you can't see where it comes from. A blow you can see, you can dodge. A blow from nowhere makes everything feel unsafe. Valmiki doesn't rush to the rescue. The first night of the war ends with the heroes down, the sky quiet, and nobody sure whether they're alive.

642.title: Indrajit's arrows
642.hook: Ravana flies Sita over the battlefield to break her, and a rakshasi friend reads the signs
642.howItsDone: Ramayana tellers remember Trijata as Sita's friend in Lanka, and often linger on her comfort over the battlefield.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's arrows. Shot from the clouds, they became serpents, and Rama and Lakshmana fell. A blow from nowhere.

Indrajit reports to his father: they're dead. Ravana is delighted, and he thinks of Sita. If she sees them lying there, she'll stop hoping, and she'll be his. So he has her put in the Pushpaka, the flying chariot, and flown out over the battlefield. Below her, among the shattered monkey army, she sees them: Rama and Lakshmana on the ground, bound and still, pierced all over with arrows. And she breaks down.
screen: `THEY'RE DEAD, FATHER.` → `SITA FLOWN OVER THE FIELD.` → `SHE BREAKS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Sita's lament in Valmiki is raw. She recalls the signs read on her body as a girl, promising she'd never be a widow, and calls them all lies. Beside her in the chariot is Trijata, a rakshasi, one of her guards from the ashoka grove, who had dreamed of Ravana's fall and told the others to leave Sita alone. Her comfort now is careful, almost like evidence in a trial. Look at their faces, she says. The faces of the dead lose their color; theirs haven't. Look at the army: if the leader were dead, they'd be scattered and running. Instead they're gathered around him, guarding him. And the last sign: this Pushpaka would not carry you if you were a widow. They're alive. So Sita is flown back to the grove, still afraid, but holding on. Down on the field, Rama wakes first. The serpents still hold him, but his eyes open, and he sees his brother beside him. His grief isn't for himself. He says he couldn't face his mother, or Sumitra, Lakshmana's mother, without him. He tells Sugriva to take the army home; the war isn't worth his friends' lives. Look at who brings hope in this chapter. Not a god, not a warrior. A rakshasi from the enemy's own household, beside a weeping prisoner, telling her the truth as she sees it. Ravana sent Sita up to lose hope, and she came back down with some.

643.title: the serpent-arrows and Garuda
643.hook: a great wind over the battlefield, and the snakes let go
643.carry: I'm your friend, don't ask why
643.howItsDone: In recitations of the Yuddha Kanda, the Garuda episode comes straight after the brothers' fall, and tellers often slow down at Garuda's refusal to say why he came.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's arrows held the brothers down, Sita was flown over them to make her despair, and Trijata read the signs of life. Your line: they're alive, and holding on.

Night on the battlefield, and the camp is out of ideas. Rama lies bound beside his brother. Sugriva wants to carry them home. Sushena, the monkey physician, says there are healing herbs on mountains far off in the ocean of milk, and someone should be sent. While they're still talking, the wind changes. A great wind comes off the sea. Clouds tear open, the waves heave, the hills shake, and trees on the shore bend flat. Something enormous is coming down out of the sky.
screen: `OUT OF IDEAS.` → `A GREAT WIND OFF THE SEA.` → `SOMETHING COMING DOWN.`

segments.voice: It's Garuda: the great eagle, king of the birds, blazing like fire. The moment the serpents feel him coming, they let go. The arrows that were snakes slither off the brothers and flee; in the old stories, serpents and Garuda are enemies. Garuda bows to the brothers and strokes their faces with his hands, and Valmiki says their wounds close at once, and they rise brighter and stronger than before. Garuda embraces them both. Rama, amazed, asks: who are you? The answer is warm, and mysterious. I'm your friend, Garutman, he says, like your own breath moving outside your body. The snakes, he explains, were sons of Kadru, the mother of serpents, made into arrows by Indrajit's sorcery. Then, just when you'd expect him to say why he's come, he doesn't. Don't ask why I'm your friend, he says, more or less. You'll understand when the battle is over. He walks around Rama in a circle of respect, and flies off into the sky. The monkey army sees the brothers standing, and roars so loud that Ravana hears it inside his palace and asks what has happened. The chapter that began in despair ends in noise. Valmiki gives no speech about rescue. He gives a wind, a bird, a touch on the face, and a friend who won't say why.

segments.voice: Remember a time help came that you didn't arrange: a neighbor at the door, a call at the right moment, a stranger who stopped. Breathe slowly and let that moment come back clearly, even if you never learned why they came.

644.title: the serpent-arrows and Garuda
644.hook: why the snakes run from Garuda, and why Garuda would come to Rama
644.howItsDone: Garuda's story from the Mahabharata's Adi Parva is often told to children, and in many Vishnu temples a figure of Garuda faces the main shrine with folded hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Garuda. A great wind, the snakes let go, a touch on the face. I'm your friend, don't ask why.

The arrows that were snakes didn't fight Garuda. The moment his wind reached the shore, they fled. People who grew up with Indian tales know why. They've heard it from grandparents, in comics, in temple carvings. It's a story about two sisters, a horse's tail, a cheat, and a son who will do anything to set his mother free. Valmiki doesn't stop to tell it, so here it is.
screen: `THE SNAKES DON'T FIGHT. THEY FLEE.` → `TWO SISTERS AND A HORSE'S TAIL.` → `A SON WHO FREES HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: It's told in the Mahabharata's first book. Two sisters, Kadru and Vinata, are both wives of the sage Kashyapa. Kadru is the mother of the serpents; Vinata is the mother of Garuda. The sisters bet on the color of a divine horse's tail, and the loser becomes the winner's servant. Kadru cheats: she has her serpent sons hang on the tail so it looks black. Vinata loses, and becomes a servant to her sister and the snakes. Her son Garuda asks the serpents what it will take to free his mother. Bring us the nectar of immortality, they say, from the gods. So Garuda storms heaven, wins the nectar, and frees her. On the way, Vishnu meets him and offers him a gift, and Garuda in turn agrees to serve Vishnu, as the bird he rides and the emblem on his banner. That's why snakes and Garuda are enemies, and why Garuda carries Vishnu. Now put that back on the battlefield at Lanka. The bird who carries Vishnu comes down to free Rama, calls himself his friend, and won't say why. For many Hindus that's a quiet sign of who Rama is: Vishnu come to earth. Valmiki doesn't spell it out here; he lets the reader notice. And so a week closes that ran from Vibhishana welcomed on the beach, to spies set free, a last offer at the gates, arrows from the sky, and a friend on the wind.
